We have a task: extract SMILES string efficiently. We have mass spec, carbon NMR, etc. Need to deduce molecule.

We have mass spec: m/z 276.066555... likely molecular ion (M+). So molecular weight ~276.07. The formula we derived from isomers: C16H20O4 (mass? Let's calculate: C16=192, H20=20, O4=64 => total 276. So matches. So formula C16H20O4.

Carbon NMR: 14 signals: 166.00,151.10,144.35,140.45,137.05,131.30 (x2),124.40,122.30,119.00,116.65 (x2),61.10,14.26. That suggests aromatic carbons (around 120-150) plus carbonyls (166) and aliphatic (61,14). So likely aromatic ring with carbonyls (esters). 14 carbons observed, but formula has 16 carbons; some overlapping signals (duplicate). Two signals at 131.30 and 116.65 duplicates maybe symmetry.

We have candidate isomers from formula list. Need to find which matches spectra.

Mass spec shows isotopic pattern: M+ at 276, then M+1 at 277 (16% relative). That suggests presence of one carbon-13? Actually natural abundance 1.1% per carbon, for 16 carbons expected ~16% M+1. So matches.

Now need to propose SMILES. Let's examine candidate isomers list from earlier (C16H20O4). The first: 'CC1(C(OC(O1)/C=C/C2=CC3=C(C=C2)OCO3)(C)C)C' That's a bicyclic? Contains many O's maybe too many O? Let's count O: OC(O1) (two O), OCO3 (two O) total 4 O. Carbons maybe 16. Contains a C=C double bond linking aromatic fused dioxole? Might have many aliphatic methyl groups (tert-butyl). Carbon NMR would have many aliphatic signals (multiple methyls). But we only see one aliphatic carbon at 14.26 (methyl) and one at 61.10 (maybe O-CH2). So not many methyls. So first candidate unlikely.

Second: 'CC(C)C1=CC(=C(C=C1)/C(=C/C(=O)C(=O)O)/O)C(C)C' This has two isopropyl groups (multiple aliphatic). Not matching.

Third: 'CCCCOC(=O)/C=C/C1=CC=C(C=C1)C(=O)OCC' This has butyl chain O-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH3 (4 carbons) plus ethoxy on acid (OCC). That would give aliphatic carbons: maybe 4+2 =6 aliphatic signals, not just one. So not match.

Fourth: 'CC1=C(C(=O)C(=C(C1=O)C)CCCOC(=O)C(=C)C)C' This seems poly carbonyl and aliphatic chain.

Fifth: 'CCC1CCCCC1OC2=CC3=C(C=C2C=O)OCO3' This has cyclohexyl etc.

Our observed aliphatic signals: 61.10 likely O-CH2 (maybe ethoxy). 14.26 methyl (maybe acetyl CH3). So maybe an acetyl group (CH3-CO-) attached to aromatic carbonyl (ester). Also carbonyl at 166 ppm (ester). So maybe a phenyl acetate? But formula C16H20O4 suggests two carbonyls (maybe diester). Could be a phenylacrylate? The carbon NMR includes 166 (ester carbonyl), 151-144 aromatic with O substituents, 131-119 aromatic, 61 (O-CH2), 14 (CH3). So maybe a phenyl propenoate with ethoxy? Wait O-CH2 at 61 typical for O-CH2 in ethoxy (CH2 attached to O). Ethoxy also has CH3 at ~14? Actually ethoxy CH3 appears ~14-15 ppm. So we have ethoxy group (CH3-CH2-O-). That gives two aliphatic carbons: CH2 at 61, CH3 at 14. Good.

Thus molecule likely contains an ethoxy ester (COOCH2CH3). That's one carbonyl (166). Another carbonyl maybe aromatic carbonyl (e.g., phenyl ketone) at 151? Actually carbonyl of aromatic ketone appears ~200. Not present. So maybe second carbonyl is part of a conjugated carbonyl (e.g., cinnamic acid derivative) giving carbonyl at 166 (maybe conjugated). But we have only one carbonyl signal at 166. So maybe only one carbonyl. But formula has O4, meaning two carbonyls (each carbonyl has O). Could be an ester (C=O) and a phenoxy (C-O) plus maybe a phenol O. O4 includes carbonyl O (2), ether O (1), phenol O (1). So only one carbonyl.

Thus structure: ethyl 4-hydroxycinnamate? That is C11H12O3? Not match.

C16H20O4 could be ethyl 4-hydroxy-3-methoxy-cinnamate? That's C11? Wait.

Let's think: aromatic ring (6 C) plus maybe another aromatic ring (6) =12. Add ethoxy (2 C) =14, plus carbonyl carbon (1) =15, plus maybe a methyl (1) =16. So maybe a phenyl acetate attached to another aromatic via a double bond? Could be a stilbene diacetate? But we have only one ethoxy.

Maybe it's ethyl 4-hydroxycinnamate with an extra methyl on aromatic (para-methyl). That would be C12? Let's compute: Cinnamic acid (C9H8O2). Ethyl ester adds C2H5O, total C11H12O3. Add hydroxy (extra O) -> C11H12O4. Need C16, so extra phenyl ring.

Maybe it's ethyl 4-(acetoxy)styrene? That would have acetoxy (CH3COO) attached to aromatic, plus ethoxy on double bond? Not.

Let's examine candidate list for C16H20O4 that have ethoxy group and aromatic. Look at third candidate: 'CCCCOC(=O)/C=C/C1=CC=C(C=C1)C(=O)OCC' This has butyl ester and ethoxy on acid, two carbonyls. Not match.

Maybe there is candidate not listed. Could generate via search but limited.

We can try to simulate spectra for some candidates to match observed carbon NMR. Let's pick candidate: 'CCOC(=O)C1=CC=CC=C1C=CC(=O)O' Not sure.

But we have carbon NMR list: 166 (ester carbonyl), 151.10 (maybe aromatic carbon attached to O (phenoxy) or conjugated carbonyl), 144-137 aromatic quaternary, 131-119 aromatic CH, 116.65 (maybe aromatic carbon attached to O?).

The presence of 151 suggests phenoxy carbon bearing OH (phenol). 151 typical for phenolic carbon (C-O). 144-137 for other quaternary aromatic.

Thus maybe a phenyl ring with two substituents: one ethoxy carbonyl (ester) attached via carbonyl to aromatic (i.e., aromatic carboxylate). Another substituent maybe a phenoxy (OH). So maybe ethyl p-hydroxycinnamate? That has formula C11H12O3? Not.

Let's compute formula for ethyl 4-hydroxycinnamate: C11H12O3? Actually cinnamic acid C9H8O2, ethyl ester adds C2H5O => C11H12O3, plus OH adds O => C11H12O4. That's C11 not C16.

Need extra phenyl ring: maybe ethyl 4-hydroxybiphenyl-3-carboxylate? That would be biphenyl (C12H9) plus carbonyl and ethoxy (C2H5O) plus OH (O). Total C16H14O3? Not.

Let's compute C16H20O4: degrees of unsaturation DBE = C - H/2 + N/2 +1 = 16 -20/2 +1 =16-10+1=7. So 7 DBE. Aromatic ring gives 4 DBE (one ring + three double). Two aromatic rings would be 8 DBE. So maybe one aromatic ring (4 DBE) plus one carbonyl (1) plus one double bond (1) plus one ring (maybe a dioxolane) etc. 7 total.

Our carbon NMR shows many aromatic signals (around 10). That suggests one aromatic ring (6 carbons) but we have many distinct signals (maybe 8-9). Could be two aromatic rings overlapping.

But we have 14 signals total, includes duplicates for symmetry. If two phenyl rings, would have 12 aromatic carbons, but we have only about 10 aromatic signals (166 is carbonyl, 151-119 about 9). So maybe one phenyl plus a heterocycle.

Let's examine candidate 1 again: 'CC1(C(OC(O1)/C=C/C2=CC3=C(C=C2)OCO3)(C)C)C' This is a tert-butyl group attached to a dioxolane fused aromatic? Contains OCH2O bridging (acetal). That would give O-CH2 at ~61, methyl at 14, plus many aromatic. Could match carbon NMR: O-CH2 (61), methyl (14). The tert-butyl would give multiple methyls (but they are quaternary carbon at 30 maybe not observed? Actually tert-butyl has three equivalent methyls giving a signal around 30, not present. So not.

Maybe the molecule is ethyl 4-hydroxy-3-methoxy cinnamate? That would have OCH3 (around 55) not observed.

Our aliphatic only two signals suggests only ethoxy group (CH3-CH2-O). So the molecule likely is an ethyl ester of a phenyl acid with additional O substituent on aromatic (like phenoxy). So formula: aromatic ring (C6H4) with two substituents: one carbonyl (COOEt) and one OH (or O-). That's C6 + carbonyl carbon (1) + ethoxy (2) =9, plus maybe additional carbon chain (like propyl) to reach C16. Not.

Maybe there is a second aromatic ring attached via O (phenoxy). That would add another C6. So total C12 aromatic + carbonyl + ethoxy = C15, need one more carbon maybe methyl on aromatic (para methyl). That would give C16. So structure could be ethyl 4-(4-methylphenoxy)benzoate? That is ethyl 4-(p-tolyl)oxybenzoate. Formula: C16H16O3? Wait count: benzoate (C7H5O2) + ethoxy (C2H5) = C9H10O2? Actually ethyl benzoate C9H10O2? No ethyl benzoate is C9H10O2? Let's compute: benzoic acid C7H6O2, plus ethyl adds C2H5 => C9H11O2? Actually ethyl benzoate formula C9H10O2? Let's check: C6H5COOCH2CH3 = C9H10O2. Yes. Add phenoxy substituent (C6H5O) attached to para position adds C6H5O, total C15H15O3? plus maybe methyl adds C1H3 => C16H18O3. Not match.

Our formula has O4, so phenoxy adds O, carbonyl adds O2, ethoxy adds O (already counted). So O4 matches.

Thus ethyl 4-(phenoxy)benzoate fits O4. Let's compute formula: Ethyl benzoate (C9H10O2) + phenoxy (C6H5O) attached to ring (replaces H) => C15H15O3? Wait we add C6H5O but lose one H from benzoate ring, so net add C6H4O. So total C9+6=15, H10+4=14, O2+1=3. That's C15H14O3. Not our formula.

Need C16H20O4, more hydrogens, more oxygens.

Maybe it's ethyl 4-(hydroxy)cinnamate with extra methyl on side chain.

Let's compute ethyl 4-hydroxycinnamate: C11H12O4 (as earlier). Need extra C5H8. Could be a tert-butyl group attached to aromatic O (as O-tert-butyl). That would add C4H9O (but O already). Not.

Given limited time, maybe the correct SMILES is one of the isomers list that matches spectra. Let's compare carbon NMR of candidate 3 (CCCCOC(=O)/C=C/C1=CC=C(C=C1)C(=O)OCC). That has two carbonyls (should show two carbonyl signals ~170 and ~200). Our data only one at 166. So not.

Candidate 1 has many signals maybe matches 14 signals? But also has tert-butyl (multiple methyl). Not.

Candidate 2 has many aliphatic.

Candidate 4: 'CC1=C(C(=O)C(=C(C1=O)C)CCCOC(=O)C(=C)C)C' This has two carbonyls (C=O) and maybe aliphatic chain.

Candidate 5: 'CCC1CCCCC1OC2=CC3=C(C=C2C=O)OCO3' This has a benzodioxole (OCO) fused, carbonyl, and cyclohexyl. Aliphatic signals many.

Thus none match simple ethoxy.

Maybe we need to generate new candidate using knowledge: SMILES for ethyl 4-hydroxycinnamate is "CCOC(=O)C=CC1=CC=C(O)C=C1". Let's compute formula: C11H12O3? Wait includes OH and carbonyl O, plus ethoxy O = O3. Actually carbonyl O2 + ethoxy O1 = O3, plus phenolic O = O4. So O4 matches. Carbons: ethoxy (2) + carbonyl carbon (1) + double bond carbon (2) + aromatic (6) =11. So C11 not C16. So not.

Thus maybe the molecule is a dimer: two aromatic rings connected via double bond (stilbene) with ethoxy carbonyl on one end. Example: ethyl trans-4-(4-hydroxyphenyl)stilbene-2-carboxylate? That would be C16H16O3? Not.

Let's compute trans-stilbene (C14H12). Add ethoxy carbonyl (C2H5O2) gives C16H17O2? plus OH adds O and H => C16H18O3. Not.

Our formula C16H20O4 has 2 more H and 1 more O than that. So maybe ethyl 4-hydroxycinnamate with an extra phenyl (makes C16). Actually trans-4-hydroxycinnamic acid (C9H8O3). Ethyl ester adds C2H5 => C11H13O3? Not.

Let's compute trans-stilbene (C14H12). Add two carbonyl O (as ester) and ethoxy adds C2H5O2 => total C16H17O2? Not.

Maybe the molecule is ethyl 4-(2-hydroxyethyl)benzoate? That would have OCH2CH2OH (adds O and 2C). Carbons: aromatic 6 + carbonyl 1 + ethoxy 2 =9 + CH2CH2 2 =11. Not.

Given difficulty, perhaps the correct answer is the SMILES we already validated: "C1COC2=C(C=CC=C2O1)C(C3=CC=C(O3)C(=O)O)O". Let's check formula: we can compute via get_formula? Not yet. Let's compute using tool.
